subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If X is a random variable with the probability distribution P(X = k) = (k + 1)c/2ᵏ for k = 0, 1, 2, …, then find c and P(1 < X < 3).

mark_split.label: Sum the series and find c

recall_prompt: Say how you would find c and P(1 < X < 3) when P(X = k) = (k + 1)c/2ᵏ — what series the probabilities make, which standard series it is, and which value of X the probability keeps.
insider_note: The range starts at k = 0, so the series opens with the term c itself — starting at k = 1 loses that term and c comes out wrong; the sum needed is 1 + 2x + 3x² + … = (1 − x)⁻², not the geometric series.

steps.label: Write ΣP = 1 as a series
steps.margin_note: First two marks. The range starts at k = 0, so the first term is (0 + 1)c/2⁰ = c. Write four terms and the dots, then take c outside: c[1 + 2(1/2) + 3(1/2)² + 4(1/2)³ + …] = 1. The coefficients 1, 2, 3, 4 identify the series used in the next step.

recall.must_convey: That ΣP(X = k) = 1 becomes c[1 + 2(1/2) + 3(1/2)² + 4(1/2)³ + …] = 1, starting from k = 0.
accept: the probabilities add to one giving c times one plus two into half plus three into half squared and so on equals one
sum of P equals one is an infinite series starting at k equals zero with coefficients one two three four
take c out, the bracket is one plus two by two plus three by four plus four by eight and so on
anni probabilities kalipithe one, c bayataki teesi one plus two into half plus three into half square plus so on
write the series from k equals zero and factor out c

steps.why: With an infinite range the condition ΣP = 1 is a series, and taking c outside the bracket exposes the coefficients 1, 2, 3, 4, … against the powers of 1/2 — the shape of a standard binomial series.
common_mistakes: Starting at k = 1 and missing the first term c.
Writing the coefficients as 1, 1, 1, … by dropping the (k + 1).
Leaving c inside every term so the pattern is hidden.

steps.label: Sum the series and find c
steps.margin_note: Three marks — the main idea. 1 + 2x + 3x² + 4x³ + … = (1 − x)⁻² for |x| < 1. With x = 1/2 the bracket is (1/2)⁻² = 2² = 4, so 4c = 1 and c = 1/4.

recall.must_convey: That the bracket is the series (1 − x)⁻² with x = 1/2, which equals 4, so 4c = 1 and c = 1/4.
accept: the series one plus two x plus three x squared is one minus x to the minus two, at x equal to half that is four, so four c is one and c is a quarter
use the binomial series for one minus x to the power minus two with x equal to half
the bracket sums to four so c equals one by four
one plus two x plus three x square series one minus x power minus two, x half pedithe four, c one by four
heard_as: one minus x to the minus two

steps.why: The series with coefficients 1, 2, 3, 4, … is the expansion of (1 − x)⁻², and 1/2 is inside its range of validity. Recognising it turns an infinite sum into one power of 2.
common_mistakes: Using the geometric series 1 + x + x² + … = (1 − x)⁻¹ and getting 2c = 1.

steps.label: Find P(1 < X < 3)
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. 1 < X < 3 on the range 0, 1, 2, … keeps only X = 2. P(X = 2) = (2 + 1)c/2² = 3c/4, and with c = 1/4 that is 3/16.

recall.must_convey: That P(1 < X < 3) is P(X = 2) alone, which is 3c/4 = 3/16.
accept: P of one less than X less than three is just P of X equals two which is three c by four equals three by sixteen

steps.why: Both inequalities are strict, and the range is integers, so exactly one value survives. The probability is one term of the given formula with the constant now known.
